# **Stetson I Mountain Wind Project Year 1 Post-Construction Monitoring Report, 2009**

for the Stetson Mountain Wind Project In Penobscot and Washington Counties, Maine

## Prepared for

First Wind Management, LLC One Dana Street, Second Floor Portland, ME  04101

Prepared by

Stantec Consulting 30 Park Drive Topsham, ME  04086

**January 2009**

## **Executive Summary**

The Stetson Mountain Wind Project in Penobscot and Washington Counties, Maine (Project) is a 57 megawatt (MW) facility.  The 38 turbines became fully operational as of January 2009. Construction on the summit of Stetson Mountain, where the turbines are located, was permitted by the Land Use Regulation Committee (LURC).  A 38-mile, 34.5 kV generator lead line was approved for the Project by the Maine Department of Environmental Protection (MDEP) and extends from the T8 R3 NBPP Township to Chester; a 115 kv electrical collection system line was built for the Project along the Stetson Mountain ridge.  The GE 1.5 sle turbines have a maximum height of 119 meters (m; 390 feet [ft]) (tower and blade-tip height combined).  Twelve of the 38 turbines are lit with Federal Aviation Administration (FAA) approved lighting.

As part of the permit conditions for the Project, post-construction monitoring was conducted by Stantec Consulting Services Inc. (Stantec), on behalf of First Wind Management, LLC (First Wind), during Year 1 of operation.  The objective of post-construction monitoring was to document impacts associated with turbine collisions for resident and migrating birds and bats in relation to the Project area.  Post-construction monitoring during 2009 involved a bird and bat mortality study, a nocturnal radar migration survey, an acoustic bat use survey, and a raptorturbine interaction and avoidance survey.  The 2009 work scope was developed by First Wind in cooperation with the Maine Department of Inland Fisheries and Wildlife (MDIFW).

## _Bird and bat mortality survey_

Bird and bat mortality searches were conducted at Stetson Mountain for 27 consecutive weeks between April 20 and October 21, 2009.  Turbine searches were conducted weekly at 19 of the 38 turbines (50 %).  Searches were also conducted at five turbines on mornings following radar surveys (“radar-mortality” searches) in the spring and fall (three of these turbines were additional to those included in the weekly searches).  Transects were spaced 3 to 4 m (10 to 13 ft) apart across the entire turbine lay-down areas, as well as adjacent roadways.  Searcher efficiency trials were conducted throughout the survey period to determine the percent of carcasses recovered by the searcher.  Scavenging rate trials were conducted to determine the percent of carcasses removed by scavengers between search intervals.

Out of 513 possible weekly turbine searches (based on weekly searches at 19 turbines for 27 weeks), a total of 506 weekly turbine searches were conducted.  An additional 79 turbine searches were conducted for the radar-mortality searches.  The searcher efficiency rate of the biologist conducting weekly searches was 56 and 50 percent for birds and bats, respectively. The percent of carcasses remaining on day 4 of the trials (the average period between carcass fall and discovery, rounded up) was 70 and 25 percent for birds and bats, respectively.

A total of 39 bird fatalities (9 were counted as incidental) were found and involved 23 different species.  The majority of birds found were passerines (n=36; 92 %); game birds – ruffed grouse ( _Bonasa umbellus_ ) - represented 5 percent of fatalities (n=2); and one raptor, a red-tailed hawk ( _Buteo jamaicensis_ ), was found by maintenance personnel.  There were seven species of state special concern among the avian fatalities: chimney swift ( _Chaetura pelagica_ ), eastern woodpewee ( _Contopus virens_ ), American redstart ( _Setophaga ruticilla_ ), black-and-white warbler

( _Mniotilta varia_ ), chestnut-sided warbler ( _Dendroica pensylvanica_ ), Tennessee warbler ( _Vermivora peregrina_ ), and yellow warbler ( _D. petechia_ ).  No state endangered or threatened species were found.  The raptor was electrocuted at a riser pole of the electrical collection system near turbine 26.  The estimate of fatality for the study year was 153 birds, 4.03 birds per turbine per study year, and 2.68 birds per megawatt per study year.

A total of five bats (all found during weekly searches) were found during the 2009 mortality searches and included the following species: little brown bat ( _Myotis lucifugus_ ) (1 pup), big brown bat ( _Eptesicus fuscus_ ) (1), hoary bat  ( _Lasiurus cinereus_ ) (2), and silver-haired bat ( _Lasionycteris noctivagans_ ), (1).  Two of the species are of special concern status in Maine: hoary bat and silver-haired bat.  The estimate of fatality for the study year was 80 bats, 2.11 bats per turbine per study year, and 1.40 bats per megawatt per study year.

There were no correlations found between bird or bat mortality and topographical setting or elevation at search turbines.  There was a significantly higher mortality of birds, bats, and birds and bats combined at turbines lit with FAA lighting.  The statistical analysis indicated that bird and bat fatalities combined were not evenly distributed among weekly searched turbines. Results were largely influenced by the number of fatalities found at turbine number 1 where 15 bird carcasses were found over the course of the study year.  The relatively high number of carcasses found at turbine number 1 was attributed to the exterior lights left on at night at the operations and maintenance building.  After six avian carcasses were found on September 30 (after a night with rain and fog conditions), First Wind requested of operations staff that the lights get turned off at night.  After that week, no other fatalities were found at turbine number 1 for the remainder of the fall surveys.  The relatively high fatality numbers at turbine 1 underscores the importance of sampling turbines located within a variety of landscape settings and with a variety of project design features.   When turbine number 1 fatalities were removed from the analysis, bird, bat, and all fatalities combined remained significantly higher at lit turbines.  However, when turbine 1 fatalities were removed from the dataset, bird, bat, and all fatalities combined were evenly distributed among search turbines with fatalities.  Without turbine 1 fatalities in the dataset, bird and bat carcasses were evenly distributed among search turbines with-and-without fatalities; when all fatalities were combined there was an uneven distribution of carcasses at turbines with-and-without fatalities.

_Nocturnal radar survey_

Nocturnal radar surveys were conducted during 20 nights in 2009, including 2 nights in spring 2009 (May 18 and May 19) and 18 nights in fall 2009 (between September 8 and October 14), to characterize nightly nocturnal migration activity in the Project area and to relate radar activity to fatalities found the following morning at five turbines within the range of detection of the radar. Surveys were conducted using X-band radar, sampling from sunset to sunrise.  Each hour of sampling included the recording of radar video files during horizontal and vertical operation. The radar was located on the summit of Stetson Mountain between turbines 19 and 20 and provided good views of turbines located both to the south and north of the survey site.

The overall passage rate for the entire fall survey period was 457 targets per kilometer per hour (t/km/hr), and nightly passage rates varied from 106 to 1,746 t/km/hr.  Mean flight direction through the Project area was 227o.  The mean flight height of targets was 420 m (1,378 ft) above the radar site, and nightly flight heights ranged from 328 m (1,076 ft) to 515 m (1,688 ft).

The percent of targets observed flying below 119 m (390 ft) was 2 percent for the entire season and varied by night, from 0 to 9 percent.

Fall radar surveys at the Project area documented patterns in nocturnal migration generally similar to those documented during pre-construction surveys conducted in the Project area, as well as other pre-construction radar surveys conducted in forested landscapes in the northeast, including highly variable passage rages between nights and a generally southwestern flight direction.  In contrast with results of other surveys, flight heights were higher and remained consistently high throughout the night, without a noticeable hourly peak.  The flight height of targets indicates that the majority of nocturnal migration in the area occurs well above the height of the wind turbines.

There were two birds found in fresh disposition (believed to have collided the night before) at turbines included in the radar-mortality searches.  These warblers were found at turbine 17, one of the turbines detected on the radar screen, on October 1.  These fatalities were believed to have collided with the turbine on the night of September 30 when weather conditions were inclement.  The mean nightly flight height on September 30 was the lowest mean nightly flight height among survey nights in the fall at 328 m.  The percentage of targets below the maximum turbine height on that night was 3 percent which is comparable to the mean seasonal percentage for targets below the maximum rotor height.  The mean nightly passage rate that night was one of the lowest documented during the fall surveys and was below the mean seasonal passage rate at 236 t/km/hr.  The radar-mortality surveys documented fatality events associated with poor weather conditions, a low mean nightly flight height, and a low mean nightly passage rate.

## _Bat detector survey_

Eight Anabat® acoustic bat detectors (Titley Electronics) were deployed in the Stetson I and II Project areas between mid-July and mid-October to document bat activity.  Two detectors were deployed on the nacelle of turbines and four detectors were deployed in trees near turbines throughout the Stetson I Project area.  Two tree detectors were deployed in the Stetson II Project area.  Data were summarized by guild and species and were tallied per detector on a nightly, hourly, and monthly basis.

At Stetson I, detectors operated properly at most detector units for most of the season, resulting in 509 detector nights of data and an 88 percent detector success rate.  During this survey period, 41 call sequences were recorded at detectors deployed at nacelle height, resulting in a detection rate of 0.3 call sequences per detector-night.  The four Stetson I detectors deployed at tree height recorded a total of 9,956 call sequences, resulting in a detection rate of 28.5 call sequences per detector-night.  Acoustic bat activity levels were generally highest in mid-August and declined steadily through mid-October, following a similar decline in nightly mean temperature.

Patterns in detection rates at tree versus high detectors are similar to the results of other regional surveys, particularly for tree detectors, which are deployed at relatively low heights

where increased bat activity levels are generally documented.  At Stetson I, the difference in species composition between detectors below tree canopy and those above tree canopy is similar to other acoustic surveys conducted in the region.  Low-frequency migratory bat species such as the hoary bat and the silver-haired bat typically comprise a higher percentage of calls recorded above tree canopy.  Many post-construction surveys have found a higher percentage of these long-distance migratory species during mortality surveys under operating wind turbines (Arnett, _et al._ 2008).  The two nacelle detectors at Stetson I recorded relatively few bats calls and most of the calls recorded at the nacelle detectors were suspected to be those of longdistance migrants.

## _Raptor migration and turbine avoidance survey_

Raptor migration and turbine avoidance surveys were conducted during 12 days in 2009, including 4 days in the spring (between April 27 and May 5) and 8 days in the fall (September 2 and October 14) to document diurnal migration activity and turbine avoidance behavior in the Project area.  Visual observation surveys were conducted from 9 am to 4 pm from prominent locations in the Project area.

A total of 70 survey hours were conducted over the spring and fall survey periods.  A total of 79 raptors, representing eleven species were observed, including 34 raptors in the spring and 45 raptors in the fall.  Red-tailed hawk, turkey vulture ( _Cathartes aura_ ), and broad-winged hawk ( _Buteo platypterus_ ) represent the most commonly observed species.  Daily counts ranged from 2 to 20 raptors and the overall passage rate was 1.13 birds/hour for the spring and fall combined.  Of raptors observed, 87 percent were observed in areas where turbines are located. Sixty-seven percent of observations of raptors within the Project area were documented at heights less than 119 m for at least a portion of their flight through the turbine areas.

During raptor migration surveys, two raptors were observed exhibiting turbine-avoidance behaviors, and during incidental observations, seven raptors were observed exhibiting turbineavoidance behaviors, including slight changes to their flight paths as they approached spinning turbines.

Two state-listed species were observed during 2009, including one state endangered species, peregrine falcon ( _Falco peregrinus_ ), and one state special concern species, northern harrier ( _Circus cyaneus_ ).  There were no bald eagles ( _Haliaeetus leucocephalus_ )) observed during the 2009 field surveys.

## **1.0 Introduction**

The Stetson Mountain Wind Project in Penobscot and Washington Counties, Maine (Project) is a 57 megawatt (MW) facility.  The 38 turbines became fully operational as of January 2009. Construction on the summit of Stetson Mountain, where the turbines are located, was permitted by the Land Use Regulation Committee (LURC).  A 38-mile, 34.5 kV generator lead line was approved for the Project by the Maine Department of Environmental Protection (MDEP) and extends from the T8 R3 NBPP Township to Chester; a 115 kv electrical collection system line was built for the Project along the Stetson Mountain ridge.

As part of the permit conditions for the Project, post-construction monitoring was conducted by Stantec, on behalf of First Wind, during Year 1 of operation.  The 2009 work scope was developed in March 2009 by First Wind in cooperation with MDIFW.  The objective of postconstruction monitoring was to document impacts associated with turbine collisions for resident and migrating birds and bats in relation to use of the Project area.  Post-construction monitoring during 2009 involved a bird and bat mortality study, a nocturnal radar migration survey, an acoustic bat use survey, and a raptor-turbine interaction and avoidance survey.

The specific objectives of each aspect of 2009 post-construction monitoring, as described in the _Stetson Mountain Wind Project Year 1 Post-Construction Monitoring Plan Work Scope_ (Appendix A), were to:

- document the Project-related fatality rates of birds and bats;

- document bat activity during peak use and peak collision-fatality periods;

- document nightly nocturnal bird migration activity using radar in order to relate activity to fatality at specific turbine locations;

- document raptor avoidance and other turbine interaction behaviors during diurnal migration; and

- to use the results of Year 1 monitoring to refine post-construction monitoring methods specific to northeastern ridge top projects including subsequent years of monitoring at Stetson Mountain.

## **1.1 PROJECT AREA DESCRIPTION**

The Stetson Mountain Wind Project is located in T8 R3 NBPP Township, Washington and Penobscot Counties, Maine (Figure 1-1).  The Project area occurs in the Maine-New Brunswick Lowlands Biophysical Region in the east region of the State, bordering New Brunswick, Canada.  The Maine-New Brunswick Lowlands Biophysical Region ranges in elevation from about 122 meters (m; 400 feet [ft]) to 182 m (600 ft), with the exception of a few mountains over 182 m (600 ft) above sea level, including Stetson Mountain at 330 m (1,085 ft).  The region includes some of the most extensive peat lands, marshes, and swamps in Maine and is the southern limit of the ribbed fen and other northern wetland systems.  The climate is relatively uniform throughout the region, with the highest average temperature in July of 79o Fahrenheit (F) and an average low temperature in January of 3o F.  The mean annual precipitation is approximately 117 centimeters (cm) (46”) (McMahon 1990).

Stetson Mountain consists of a 9.7-kilometer (6 mile) long ridgeline generally oriented north to south.  Timber harvesting is a common land use in the area and the natural community of the Project area has been influenced by recent forest harvesting.  Northern hardwood and mixed conifer are the dominant forest-types in the region (McMahon 1990); the forest cover on Stetson Mountain is largely mixed northern hardwoods.

The 38 GE 1.5 sle turbines have a maximum height of 119 m (390 ft) (tower and blade-tip height combined).  The turbines have a maximum rotor-blade diameter of 77 m (252 ft).  The turbines activate at a wind speed of 3.5 meters/second (m/s) and stop at a maximum wind speed of 25 m/s.  Twelve of the 38 turbines are lit by L-864 red flashing FAA lighting (Figure 1-1).

The turbines are generally positioned north-to-south along the ridgeline of Stetson Mountain. Turbine 1 is located next to the operations and maintenance building.  Turbine lay-down areas created during construction have a typical diameter of 76 m (250 ft).  Cleared areas and steep side slopes were covered with crushed stone after construction.  The flat construction areas have been reclaimed using the original topsoil, hydro-seeded, and mulched with hay.  The turbine driveways and the base of the towers consist of gravel and crushed stone.

## **2.0 BIRD AND BAT MORTALITY SEARCHES**

## **2.1 DATA COLLECTION METHODS**

## **2.1.1 Mortality Search Methods**

Bird and bat mortality searches were conducted at Stetson Mountain for 27 consecutive weeks between April 20 and October 21, 2009.  This timeframe covered four distinct seasons:

- Spring migration (April 20 to May 31)

- Summer (June 1 to July 12)

- Late-summer (July 13 to August 24)

- Fall migration (August 25 to October 21)

Turbine searches were conducted weekly at 19 of the 38 turbines (50 %) (Figure 2-1). Selection of search turbines was randomized but also included those turbines centered with relatively large cleared lay-down areas as well as turbines in different topographic settings (crest, saddle, mid-slope, and end turbines).

Similar to other bird and bat mortality studies conducted on forested ridgelines in the east, mortality search effort focused primarily on the cleared and leveled turbine lay-down areas. Turbines relatively centered in the lay-down areas were included in weekly searches in order to increase the detection of carcasses that may fall on all sides of the turbines.  Transects were spaced 3 to 4 m (10 to 13 ft) apart across the entire turbine lay-down areas, as well as adjacent roadways.  For consistency, all transects were oriented east-to-west.  The start and end points of each transect were marked along the edge of the plot (with flagging on trees or wooden stakes, or spray paint on rocks).

A Stantec biologist conducted the weekly searches and it generally took three survey days to complete searches at the 19 turbines.  During searches, the surveyor would walk slowly, searching on both sides of transects for bird or bat fatalities.  Any fatality found along or between transects was documented.  All intact bird or bat carcasses or remnants of scavenged carcasses (a cluster of feathers representing more than a molt, or a patch of skin and bone) were documented as fatalities.

For each fatality found, the following information was recorded on standardized datasheets:

- turbine number;

- carcass distance from turbine (determined with a laser range finder);

- carcass direction from turbine (compass reading);

- carcass distance and direction from observer when found;

- date;

- surveyor;

- time discovered;

- ground conditions (vegetation type and height, wet, dry, etc.);

- species identification (including age and sex when possible);

- carcass position;

- stage of decomposition of the carcass (previous night, 2 to 3 days, 4 to 7 days, 7 to14 days, greater than 2 weeks);

- evidence of scavenger activity; and

- additional notes when necessary.

Carcasses were collected and frozen.  To the extent possible, casualties believed to be associated with the wind farm were distinguished from those believed to be associated with the electrical collection system line, vehicle collisions, or natural sources of mortality.  Those birds that were found heavily scavenged or were otherwise unidentifiable to species were sent to the Smithsonian National Museum of Natural History for feather or DNA identification.

Ground conditions including cover type and vegetation type were documented weekly at each of the search turbines.

On those nights prior to mortality searches, sky conditions - including cloud height, cloud type, and percent cloud cover - were recorded from Lincoln, Maine.  Additional weather information – wind speed, wind direction, air temperature, and barometric pressure – were collected from a met tower and a turbine nacelle in the Project area.

## **2.1.2 Additional Turbine Searches**

Bird and bat mortality searches were conducted at a sub-set of turbines on mornings following nocturnal radar migration surveys in the spring and fall.  Mortality searches were conducted at five turbines which were visible in the range of detection of the radar unit; two of these turbines were included in the regular weekly turbine searches (Figure 2-1).  The remaining three turbines were additional turbines.  For clarification, this subset of turbines will be referred to as ‘radarmortality search’ turbines while those involved in regular weekly searches will be referred to as ‘weekly search’ turbines.  On some occasions, the radar-mortality searches were conducted by a biologist searching with a leashed dog[2] .  The objectives, methods, and results of the radar surveys and corresponding mortality searches are included in Section 5.0 of this report.

During the fall, First Wind requested that the remainder of turbines not included in weekly searches or radar-mortality searches be surveyed.  Therefore, over the course of the survey

year, all turbines at Stetson Mountain were searched at least once.  Some of these ‘additional’ turbine searches were conducted by a biologist searching with a leashed dog.

## **2.1.3 Incidental Mortality Findings and Wildlife Observations**

Any fatalities found by maintenance personnel or by surveyors outside of the weekly searches were documented as incidental and were removed from the study area.  These findings were reported as incidental and were not included in the estimates of total mortality for birds and bats; however, these findings were included in the spatial and temporal summary of bird and bat fatalities.

While surveyors were on-site for mortality searches, incidental wildlife-turbine interaction observations were documented on standardized datasheets.  The date, species, location, proximity to Project structures, and description of the animal’s general activity - particularly any interactions to turbines – were recorded.

## **2.1.4 Searcher Efficiency Trials**

The objective of searcher efficiency trials was to estimate the percent of bird and bat carcasses that may go undetected during weekly searches.  Searcher efficiency trials, unannounced to the surveyor, were conducted throughout the survey period.  The study targeted the use of 25 trial carcasses, of native species, over the course of the survey year.  There were four separate trials conducted throughout the survey period to account for changes in ground conditions over the course of the survey period.  Trials were initiated on: 1) April 28, 2) June 15, 3) July 10, and 4) September 10.

On the morning of trials, the project manager left out carcasses early in the morning at turbines scheduled to be searched that day.  Carcasses were placed in search plots within a variety of ground cover types (clover and grass at a variety of heights, bare gravel and rock, sparse grass and rock).  Small and large bat carcasses, and small and large bird carcasses, at varying stages of decomposition, were placed during trials.  Carcasses were discreetly marked with string or an elastic band so that, when found, the surveyor would be able to distinguish trial carcasses from actual fatalities.  Trial carcasses recovered by the surveyor were collected.  After the test, the project manager picked up any carcasses not found by the surveyor and determined the number of carcasses recovered by the surveyor.

## **2.1.5 Scavenging Rate Trials**

Scavenging rate trials were conducted to determine the percent of carcasses removed by scavengers between search intervals.  The study targeted the use of 25 trial carcasses in good disposition (fresh disposition but previously frozen), of native species, over the course of the survey year.  Two separate trials were conducted once at the beginning of the survey year and once at the end of the survey year to account for seasonal variation in scavenger activity.  Trials were initiated on: 1) June 1 and 2) October 5.  The trials used small, medium, and large bird carcasses, and small and large bat carcasses.  Carcasses were discreetly marked with string or elastic band to distinguish trial birds and bats from actual fatalities.  During trials, carcasses were placed at turbines throughout the study area, and within a variety of ground cover types.

The status of the carcasses was monitored daily over a period of 14 days.  All evidence of insect, mammalian, or avian scavenging was noted on standardized datasheets.  A carcass was considered present if it was partially scavenged but still readily detectable to a surveyor.  A

carcass was considered absent if it was completely removed or few feathers or other remains were left so that it was not readily detectable.  All remaining carcasses were removed from search plots on day 14.

## **2.1.6 Statistical Analysis**

Analysis of the seasonal timing of fatalities, the comparison of fatality events with weather conditions, and the summary of the distances carcasses were found from turbines considered all carcasses found during the study (i.e. including incidental findings).  Survey effort varied among all turbines (weekly searched turbines verses radar-mortality search turbines verses additional turbines searched once per survey year) and therefore was considered when interpreting the results.  However, the statistical analysis of the spatial distribution of fatalities and the estimate of fatality rates for birds and bats considered only those carcasses found during the weekly searches.

_Seasonal timing of all fatalities (including incidentals)_

Bird and bat fatalities were summarized according to the seasonal timing of collision events.

_Fatality event and weather condition comparisons (including incidentals)_

For those birds and bats found fresh (collision event believed to have occurred the night prior to the search), weather conditions were summarized for the night of collision.

_Spatial distribution of fatalities (only carcasses found during weekly searches)_

Analysis of the spatial distribution of fatalities included a summary of:

- the evenness of distribution of fatalities at individual turbines;

- the location of the fatalities at FAA lit verses unlit turbines;

- the location of fatalities at turbines with varying sizes of search area (cleared and leveled turbine lay-down areas);

- the location of fatalities at turbines with different landscape features including topographical setting (crest, saddle, side-slope), as well as turbines at different elevations; and

- the average distance of bird and bat fatalities from towers.

SAS 9.1 (SAS Institute, Inc., Cary, North Carolina) was used to compare bird and bat fatalities with landscape and turbine design characteristics.  Nonparametric tests were used in all cases to account for non-normal data.  Chi-square tests were run to determine if bird, bat, and all fatalities combined were evenly distributed among turbines.  This analysis was first run with weekly searched turbines that had fatalities, then with weekly searched turbines both with-andwithout fatalities.  Bird, bat, and all fatalities combined were compared between lit and unlit turbines using Wilcoxon Rank-Sum tests.  Spearman correlations were used to test whether bird, bat, and all fatalities combined were linearly associated with size of search area and turbine elevation.  Bird, bat, and all fatalities combined were compared among turbines in three different topographical settings (crest, side-slope, saddle) using Kruskal-Wallis tests.  A significance level of 0.05 was chosen prior to analysis.

## _Estimate of fatality rates_

The results of the four separate searcher efficiency trails were pooled for bird and bat carcasses.  The searcher efficiency rate was determined as the total number of carcasses found divided by the total number of carcasses placed.

The results of the two scavenging rate trials were pooled for bird and bat carcasses.  Jain _et al._ (2007, 2008, 2009a) noted that the period between carcass fall and discovery is approximately half the actual search interval, rounded up.  For a seven-day search interval, this period is 4 days.  Therefore, the analysis factored the percent of trial carcasses that remained visible on day 4.

The estimate of bird and bat mortality rates (fatalities per turbine per study year, and fatalities per megawatt per study year) for the Project, was modeled after methods described by Jain _et al._ (2007, 2008, 2009a).  The total estimate of mortality per study year (ĉ) was based on the total number of birds and bats found (C), the proportion of turbines searched (Ps), the percent of carcasses found by the surveyor (Se), and the percent of carcasses not removed by scavengers (Sc).

_The variance was also calculated as described by Jain_ et al _. (2007, 2008, 2009a)._

The standard deviation was then calculated based on the square root of the variance divided by the square root of the number of searched turbines, multiplied by a factor of 95 percent confidence (1.96).

## **2.2.5 Spatial distribution of fatalities**

Bird fatalities were found at 15 different turbines (35 bird carcasses at weekly searched turbines, 3 at other turbines, and 1 at the electrical collection system line).  The number of bird fatalities at individual turbines ranged from 1 to 4 birds, with the exception of turbine number 1 (Figure 2-2).  There were 15 birds (38 % of all avian fatalities) found over the course of the study year at turbine 1.  Notably, there were 6 bird carcasses found on September 30.  These birds were of a fresh disposition and were believed to have collided with the turbine the previous night during rain and fog conditions.  These fatalities were believed to be associated with the exterior lights that were on at the operations and maintenance facility which is located within 75 m of turbine number 1[4] (Figure 2-2).  The Chi-square test determined that bird fatalities were not evenly distributed among search turbines with fatalities (X-square=58.60, d.f.=11).  Also, bird fatalities were not evenly distributed among search turbines with-and-without fatalities (Xsquare=113.2, d.f.=18).

Bat fatalities were found at 4 different turbines; each of these turbines was a weekly search turbine.  Bat fatalities at individual turbines ranged from 1 to 2 bats (Figure 2-2).  Bat fatalities were evenly distributed among search turbines with fatalities (X-square=0.60, d.f.=3); however, bat fatalities were not evenly distributed among search turbines with-and-without fatalities (Xsquare=21.6, d.f.=18).

Additionally, bird and bat fatalities combined were not evenly distributed among search turbines with fatalities (X-square=66.24, d.f.=11).  For all fatalities combined, bird and bat fatalities were not evenly distributed among search turbines with-and-without fatalities (X-square=107.25, d.f.=18).

When turbine number 1 fatalities were removed from the analysis, bird fatalities were evenly distributed among search turbines with fatalities (X-square = 6.4, d.f. = 10), bat fatalities were evenly distributed among search turbines with fatalities (X-square = 0.60, d.f. = 3), and all fatalities combined were evenly distributed among search turbines with fatalities (X-square = 15.16, d.f. = 10).  For search turbines with-and-without fatalities, excluding turbine number 1 fatalities, bird fatalities were evenly distributed (X-square = 23.2, d.f. = 17).  Bat fatalities were evenly distributed (X-square = 20.2, d.f. = 17); however, all fatalities combined were not evenly distributed (X-square = 36.2, d.f. = 17).

## **2.3 DISCUSSION**

Although there was grass and clover growth in search areas that were seeded after construction, searcher efficiency was relatively high at Stetson Mountain compared to the searcher efficiency rates reported for other recent mortality studies conducted on ridgelines in the region: searcher efficiency for birds and bats at Mars Hill, Maine during 2007 was 56 and 50 percent, respectively; it was 38 and 42 percent in 2008 at Mars Hill; 41.2 percent for bats (not calculated for birds) at Buffalo Mountain, Tennessee in 2007; and 85 percent for large birds, 68 percent for small birds, and 58.6 for bats at Mount Storm, West Virginia in 2008 (Stantec 2008, Stantec 2009, Fielder _et al._ 2007, Young _et al._ 2009).  There were no vegetation management activities conducted during the 2009 searches; however, as vegetation growth continues to spread and thicken within search plots during consecutive seasons it may reduce searcher efficiency.

Estimates of avian fatalities reported for studies conducted in the east and upper Midwest, have ranged from 0.33 birds/turbine/year (low range of estimates from Buffalo Ridge, Minnesota 1995) to 9.48 birds/turbine/year (high range of estimates from Maple Ridge, New York 2006) (Table 2-7).  The estimate for bird mortality at Stetson Mountain falls within this range.   Avian fatalities involved 23 different species, 7 of which were special concern in the state of Maine. There was one individual of each special concern avian species found with the exception of two black-and-white warblers. The majority of birds involved with collisions at Stetson Mountain were passerines, mainly neo-tropical migrants.  The dates that avian fatalities were found indicated that the majority of collisions occurred during nocturnal migration during the spring and fall; however, a few fatalities were documented during the breeding season.  The results of the Stetson Mountain mortality study are consistent with the findings of other mortality studies in the region in terms of species involved in collisions, seasonal timing of the majority of collisions, and the number of individuals involved in collisions (NRC 2007).  Studies suggest that nocturnal migrant passerines are more susceptible to collision (NRC 2007).  This is likely influenced by the relatively high abundance of passerines as well as their migration flight behaviors. However, common species within this avian group are less susceptible to population-level impacts than other avian groups, such as raptors, due to their relatively high abundance and relatively high annual recruitment.

Emerging bat fatality data suggests that latitude, or geographic location, may influence bat mortality at wind farms as notably higher estimates of bat kills per turbine per year have been documented in the southeastern US, particularly along forested ridgelines, and lower in other regions such as the Rocky Mountains or the Pacific Northwest (Arnett _et al._ 2008, Arnett 2005, Fielder _et al._ 2007).  Bat mortality in the eastern US has ranged from 0.17 bats/turbine/year (low range of estimates from Mars Hill, Maine 2008) to 63.9 bats/turbine/year (Buffalo Mountain, Tennessee 2005) (Table 2-7).  Bat mortality at Stetson Mountain was low compared to mortality at other wind farms in the east, and comparable to bat mortality detected at Mars Hill Maine.  It should be noted that regional differences in bat habitat and populations limit the value of direct comparison among different regions in the east.

Species composition of bat fatalities at Stetson Mountain is consistent with the findings of other studies in the region (Arnett et al. 2008).  There were 4 different species of bat involved in collisions at Stetson Mountain, two of which are listed as special concern in the state of Maine.  There was one individual of each bat species found with the exception of two hoary bats. The majority of bat fatalities at Stetson Mountain were detected in August, consistent with the timing of the peak period of bat mortality in the region (Arnett _et al._ 2008).  The majority of bat fatalities at wind farms around the world involve migratory bats during fall migration (Arnett _et al_ . 2008, Baerwald and Barclay 2009).

There were no correlations found between bird or bat mortality and topographical setting or elevation at search turbines.  There was a significantly higher mortality of birds, bats, and birds and bats combined at turbines lit with FAA lighting.  These results are inconsistent with the findings of the majority of other studies which have shown no relationship between bird and bat mortality and FAA lit turbines (Jain _et al._ 2009a, Arnett 2005, NRC 2007).  There were only 5 bat fatalities found, all of which occurred at FAA lit turbines.  This is a small sample size and therefore difficult to draw conclusions from.  The relationship between bird fatalities and turbines with FAA lighting is somewhat influenced by the number of birds found at turbine number 1 next to the operations and maintenance facility.  However, after turbine number 1 is removed from the dataset, the average number of fatalities at lit turbines remains higher than at unlit turbines, and bird, bat, and all fatalities combined remained significantly higher at lit turbines than unlit turbines.  This relationship between fatalities and lit turbines should be further tested for in future monitoring at Stetson Mountain.

There has been some concern as to whether sampling all turbines at a Project or sub-sampling turbines that are representative of the Project area is appropriate for the first year of monitoring at wind projects in Maine.  The concern is that sub-sampling may not be able to account for turbines that may be outliers in terms of the numbers of fatalities. One of the objectives of the Stetson Mountain 2009 monitoring study was to investigate the suitability of sampling fifty percent of turbines versus all turbines at the Project.  Therefore, the evenness of distribution of carcasses among turbines included in weekly searches was tested for.  The analysis indicated that bird and bat fatalities combined were not evenly distributed among weekly searched turbines.  Results were largely influenced but the number of fatalities found at turbine number 1 where 15 bird carcasses were found.  The relatively high number of carcasses found at turbine number 1 was attributed to the exterior lights left on at night at the operations and maintenance building.  After 6 avian carcasses were found on September 30 (after a night with rain and fog conditions), First Wind Environmental Affairs requested of Operations that the lights be turned off at night when no staff were present at the facility.  After that week, no other fatalities were found at turbine number 1 for the remainder of the fall surveys.  There were no other turbines in direct vicinity of a building with exterior lighting and there were no other turbines with relatively large numbers of carcasses.

The Mars Hill Wind Farm 2-year fatality dataset, where all turbines were searched during both years of surveys, is available to investigate the effectiveness of sampling all turbines verses sub-sampling.  Chi-square goodness of fit tests were performed on the Mars Hill bird and bat fatality data from 2007 and 2008.  At Mars Hill, all turbines were searched weekly during both years of study.  The analysis was run on observed fatalities at each turbine (the number of fatalities found and not corrected by any factors such as searcher efficiency or scavenger carcass removal) to determine whether the number of carcasses found at each turbine differed significantly from what was expected.  There was no significant difference between the number

of observed bat or bird carcasses found at each turbine and the number of expected bat or bird carcasses during 2007 or 2008 (Table 2-8), indicating that observed carcasses were found evenly among turbines during each of the survey years.  There was, however, a significant difference when bird carcasses from 2007 and 2008 were pooled (Table 2-8), meaning carcasses were not evenly distributed among turbines when the two years were combined.  This may indicate that the carcasses observed were found at different turbines among the two years, and that carcass distribution at turbines among the study years was random.  This supports the conclusions that there is no topographical, landscape, or habitat features which influenced mortality at Mars Hill.  These results are consistent with other studies conducted along forested ridgelines in the east (Kerns and Kerlinger 2004, Arnett 2005, Fielder _et al_ . 2007).

There have been several statistical methods used to estimate post-construction mortality todate, and newer methods are being developed all the time.  The estimator for the Mars Hill 2007 and 2008, and the Stetson Mountain 2009 data is based on methods used by Jain _et al._ (2007, 2008, 2009a) and was used in the interest of comparability of fatality estimates.  Regardless of the method chosen, all methods currently function by taking the number of carcasses actually found and adjusting those numbers based on estimates of detection probability, proportion of turbines searched, and other factors.  For typical bird and bat mortality studies, mortality is estimated at the Project-level by determining average estimates based on the results of subsampling turbines, or searching all turbines at small projects, then applying a per-turbine fatality estimate evenly to all turbines.  Sub-sampling does not necessarily allow for the detection of turbines with ‘out-lying’ numbers of fatalities.  However, by sampling turbines which have a variety of landscape and project design features, factors that may influence higher or lower fatality rates at the individual turbine level may be investigated.

Carcasses were found to be unevenly distributed among turbines at Stetson Mountain; however, this was believed to be influenced by the anomaly of turbine number 1’s location next to the operations and maintenance facility which was lit with exterior lighting at night.  The study design at Stetson was able to detect the uneven distribution of fatalities among turbines, suggesting that searching a proportion of turbines which are representative of all landscape and project design features, as well as any other factors that could increase risk at particular turbines, provides a survey effort rigorous enough to detect anomalies.  Therefore, it may be that sampling all turbines is not necessary for these types of monitoring studies when turbines included in searches are adequately representative of the Project.  The relatively high fatality numbers at turbine 1 underscores the importance of sampling turbines located within a variety of landscape settings and with a variety of project design features when survey effort includes sub-sampling of turbines to document variability of fatalities among turbines and to estimate the overall Project fatality rate for birds and bats.

## **3.0 Nocturnal Radar Survey**

The majority of North American passerines (songbirds) migrate at night and the strategy of migrating at night may have evolved to take advantage of more stable atmospheric conditions for their flapping flight (Kerlinger 1995).  Additionally, migration during the night, with cooler nighttime temperatures, may provide a more efficient medium to regulate body temperature during more active, flapping flight and reduce predation risk while in flight (Alerstam 1990, Kerlinger 1995).  Documenting the patterns of nocturnal migrants requires the use of radar or other non-visual technologies.  As part of Year-1 post-construction monitoring at the Stetson Mountain Wind Project, nocturnal radar surveys were conducted in the Project area during spring and fall 2009.

The goals of the 2009 radar survey at Stetson Mountain were to:

- document and calculate nightly passage rates, flight direction, and flight altitude; and

- determine if migrant use and fatality appear to be related and, if so, how.

The survey targeted sampling on 20 nights, with the majority of sampling allocated for the fall; and targeted nights with weather conditions suitable for large migration movements as well as nights with inclement conditions (fog or rain) when risk of collision is increased.  A survey location allowing for the detection of at least five turbines on the radar screen was chosen in an effort to determine if nocturnal migrant use, as documented by the radar, and fatality are related. The scope of work (as described in Appendix A) was developed by First Wind in conjunction with MDIFW.

Radar surveys were conducted from sunset to sunrise on 2 nights in spring 2009 (May 18 and 19, 2009) and 18 nights in fall 2009 (between September 8 and October 14, 2009).  The radar was deployed at the summit of Stetson Mountain between turbines 19 and 20 (Figures 3-1, 3-2), at an elevation of 360 m (1,180 ft).  The radar was oriented northeast-to-southwest so that in vertical mode, the antennae would sweep along the ridgeline.  This location provided a good view in most directions, and allowed for detection of five turbines (18, 17, 16, 15, and 14) south of the radar unit and five turbines north of the unit (21, 22, 23, 24, and 25).  Turbines 19 and 20 were next to the radar unit and, due to ground clutter, were not visible on the radar screen. Although the radar’s view was partially obscured in some areas of the radar detection range, targets could be tracked as they moved in and out of those areas (Figures 3-3, 3-4).

## **3.1 DATA COLLECTION METHODS**

## **3.1.1 Radar Data**

Marine surveillance radar, similar to that described by Cooper _et al._ (1991), was used during field data collection.  The radar has a peak power output of 12 kilowatts (kW) and has the ability to track small animals, including birds, bats, and even insects, based on settings selected for the radar functions.  It cannot, however, readily distinguish between different types of animals being detected.  Consequently, all animals observed on the radar screen were identified as “targets.”  The radar has an “echo trail” function which captures past echoes of flight trails, enabling determination of flight direction.  During all operations, the radar’s echo trail was set to 30 seconds.  The radar was equipped with a 2 m (6.5 ft) waveguide antenna, deployed 7 m (25 ft) above ground.  The antenna has a vertical beam height of 20o (10o above and below horizontal), and the front end of the antenna was inclined approximately 5o to increase the proportion of the beam directed into the sky.

Objects on the ground detected by the radar cause returns on the radar screen (echoes) that appear as blotches called ground clutter.  Large amounts of ground clutter reduce the ability of the radar to track birds and bats flying over those areas (Figure 3-3).

**Figure 3-3.** An example of ground clutter causing objects in horizontal mode (top) and vertical mode (bottom).  Although the radar records three-dimensional space, it is translated by the radar screen into a two dimensional representation, which can cause targets to be obscured from view.

However, vegetation and hilltops near the radar can be used to reduce or eliminate ground clutter by “hiding” clutter-causing objects from the radar.  These nearby features also cause ground clutter, but their proximity to the radar antenna generally limits the ground clutter to the center of the radar screen – targets are indistinguishable from the “clutter” as represented on the radar screen (Figure 3-4).  However, targets traveling into and out of the ground clutter areas can be tracked.  The presence or reduction of potential clutter producing objects was carefully considered during site selection and radar station configuration.

**Figure 3-4.** Proper site selection can reduce ground clutter to the center of the radar screen (bottom), so that the majority of the two-dimensional radar screen remains relatively uncluttered, allowing targets to be tracked as they both enter and leave the cluttered area (top; horizontal screenshot is on the left and vertical is on the right).

Because the anti-rain function of the radar must be turned down to detect small songbirds and bats, surveys could not be conducted during active rainfall.  Therefore, surveys were planned largely for nights without rain.  However, in order to characterize migration patterns during nights without optimal conditions, some nights with weather forecasts including occasional showers, mist, or fog were sampled.

The radar was operated in two modes throughout the course of each night.  In surveillance mode, the antenna spins horizontally to survey the airspace around the radar and detects the number of targets and their flight direction as they pass through the Project Site (Figure 3-4). By analyzing the echo trail, the flight direction and flight speed of targets can be determined.

In vertical mode, the radar unit is tilted 90o to vertically survey the airspace above the radar (Harmata _et al._ 1999).  In vertical mode, target echoes do not provide directional data, but do provide information on the altitude of targets passing through the vertical, 20o radar beam (Figure 3-5).  Both modes of operation were used during each hour of sampling.

**Figure 3-5** .  Detection range of the radar in vertical mode

The radar was operated at a range of 1.4 km (0.75 nautical miles) to ensure detection of small targets.  When radar is operated at ranges greater than 1.4 km, larger birds can be detected but the echoes of small birds are reduced in size and restricted to a smaller portion of the radar screen, thus limiting the ability to observe the movement pattern of individual targets; consequently, 1.4 km is the appropriate detection range for this type of study.

The radar display was connected to the video recording software of a computer enabling digital archiving of the radar data for subsequent analysis.  This software recorded and archived video samples continuously every hour from sunset to sunrise of each survey night.  By alternating the radar antenna every ten minutes from vertical mode to horizontal mode, a total of 30 minutes of vertical samples and 30 minutes of horizontal samples were collected within each hour.  A stratified random sample set was developed by randomly selecting 6 horizontal samples and 6 vertical samples per hour of survey.  This sampling schedule allowed for randomization of sample selection and prevented double-counting of targets due to the 30-second echo trail used to determine the flight path vector.

## **3.1.2 Mortality Searches**

On mornings following radar surveys, mortality searches were conducted at turbines 15, 16, 17, 18, and 21 which were visible on the radar screen (Figure 2-1).  Methods used during post-radar mortality searches were the same as those used for standard mortality searches as described in Section 2.0.

## **3.1.3 Weather Data**

Temperature, wind speed and direction were recorded on an hourly basis by a meteorological tower located at the north end of the Project, near turbine 37, as well as from the nacelle of turbine 30 for the duration of the radar survey period.  The mean, maximum, and minimum temperature, mean and maximum wind speed, and mean wind direction were calculated for each night.  This information was used during data analysis to help characterize any patterns in migration activity for particular nights and for the season overall.

## **3.1.4 Night Vision and Ceilometer Data**

A night vision device (NVD) is an optical instrument that allows objects to be seen in near darkness by enhancing ordinary ambient light, usually from the moon and stars, which is reflected by objects in the scene being viewed.  NVDs contain an image intensifier tube that amplifies very weak light.  To enhance the distance the observer can see, night vision observations can be supplemented by directing a one-million candlepower spotlight (ceilometer) fixed with a red filter lens vertically into the sky in a manner similar to that described by Gauthreaux (1969).  The range of detection with this method is approximately 150 m (49 ft ft), which is just above the maximum height of the turbines at Stetson Mountain.

On two nights in the spring and eight nights in the fall, NVD and ceilometer (with a red filter lens) surveys were conducted at the radar site to document and characterize low-flying targets.  The focal point for the beam was either turbine 19 or turbine 20.  Surveys were conducted over 20 minute periods during the first 2 to 6 hours of radar sampling.  A total of 240 minutes of nocturnal visual surveys were conducted in the spring, and 560 minutes were conducted in the fall.  All birds, bats, or insects observed with the NVD were recorded.  A monocular NVD was used and mounted on the observers head for hands-free use with a harness attachment (i.e., night-vision goggles).  The ceilometer was held in-hand to facilitate night vision tracking, as necessary, of any birds, bats, or insects passing in the vicinity of the survey focal points.  Visual data was used during data analysis to help characterize activity of insects, birds, and bats that were in the air during that hour and for the night overall.

## **3.2 DATA ANALYSIS METHODS**

## **3.2.1 Radar Data**

Video samples were analyzed using a digital analysis software tool developed by Stantec.  For horizontal samples, targets (either birds or bats) were differentiated from insects based on their flight speed.  Following adjustment for wind speed and direction, targets traveling faster than approximately 6 m (20 ft) per second were identified as a bird or bat target (Larkin 1991, Bruderer and Boldt 2001).  The software tool recorded the time, location, and flight vector for each target traveling fast enough to be a bird or bat within each horizontal sample, and these results were output to an Excel spreadsheet.  For vertical samples, the software tool recorded the entry point of targets passing through the vertical radar beam, the time, and flight altitude above the radar location, and then subsequently outputs the data to a spreadsheet.  These datasets were then used to calculate passage rate (reported as targets per kilometer of migratory front per hour), flight direction, and flight altitude of targets.

Mean target flight directions (± 1 circular standard deviation) were summarized using software designed specifically to analyze directional data (Oriana2[©] Kovach Computing Services).  The statistics used for this analysis are based on those used by Batschelet (1965), because they take into account the circular nature of the data.

Flight altitude data were summarized using linear statistics.  Mean flight altitudes (± 1 standard error [SE]) were calculated by hour, night, and overall season.  The percent of targets flying below 119 m (390 ft), the maximum height of the turbines with blades, was also calculated hourly, for each night, and for the entire survey period.

During analysis of radar sample files, if a flight vector of a target was observed to intersect with the screen clutter representing a turbine blade, that sample was marked as a potential turbine interaction.  The number of video samples with potential turbine interactions was summarized[5] .

The average nightly flight height ranged from 328 ± 16 m (1076 ± 52 ft) on September 30 to 515 ± 16 (1688 ± 52 ft) on October 5 (Figure 3-9; Appendix C, Table 3).  The percent of targets observed flying below 119 m (390 ft), the maximum turbine height, was two percent for the entire season and varied nightly from zero to nine percent (Figure 3-10).  For the entire season, the mean hourly flight heights were consistently between 400 and 450 m from the second to thirteenth hour (Figure 3-11).

No other carcasses were found in conjunction with radar-mortality searches (one warbler was found after a night of radar sampling in the spring although its disposition was aged and was not believed to have collided the night prior during radar sampling).

## **3.3.6 Night Vision and Ceilometer Data, Spring and Fall**

During nocturnal visual observations, one bat was observed in the spring; six birds, five bats, and three targets that could not be identified as bird or bat were documented in the fall (Appendix C, Table 4).  No target-turbine interactions were observed during nocturnal visual observations.

## **3.4 DISCUSSION**

The results of this field survey provide useful information about site-specific migration activity and patterns in the Project area, especially when the results are compared with pre-construction surveys conducted in the Project area, as well as other previous studies conducted in the vicinity and in the region.  Currently, there is no reliable way to distinguish birds from bats during radar data analysis, so results refer only to “targets.”  Given that the number of potential bird species migrating across the Project area far outweighs the number of species of bats known to occur in Maine, it is likely that the pool of observed targets is composed of a higher percentage of birds than bats.  Therefore, results are discussed here primarily in the context of bird migration.

One of the survey objectives was to document nightly passage rates, flight direction, and flight altitude.  Passage rates varied greatly between nights throughout the survey period (September 8 to October 14) indicating migration occurred in pulses, with rates of migration likely influenced by weather patterns and conditions from night to night.  In comparison, flight heights remained fairly consistent throughout the survey period, with most mean hourly flight heights documented above 400 m above the radar location.  During the survey period, fewer than 20 hours had mean hourly flight heights less than 300 m above the radar location and no hourly flight heights were less than 200 m above the radar location.  The generally southwestern flight direction observed during the fall is expected during fall migration and is comparable to most publicly available pre-construction radar survey results in the northeast.

Overall the results of the fall 2009 survey were similar to the results of the fall 2006 surveys conducted in the Project area (Table 3-2).  The seasonal mean passage rate in fall 2009 was slightly lower than in fall 2006 and the seasonal mean flight height in fall 2009 was slightly higher than in fall 2006.  The flight direction was exactly the same in both seasons.  Between the two seasons, the nightly range and seasonal mean of percent of targets observed below maximum turbine height was substantially lower in fall 2009 than in fall 2006.
